name: The Robe Spellbooks of High Sorcery

pages.name: Using the Robe Spellbooks
pages.html:
The Orders of High Sorcery do not merely disagree about ethics. They train the mind in different directions, and over centuries those habits have produced three recognisable magical traditions.

Magic is one art beneath three moons. The robe does not change the source of magic; it changes what the wizard is taught to seek within it.

Wayreth teaching maxim

The School Matrix

OrderFavoured schoolsWorking principle
White RobesAbjuration, Divination, EnchantmentProtect, reveal, and strengthen voluntary choice.
Red RobesConjuration, Illusion, TransmutationChange the terms of a problem rather than simply overpower it.
Black RobesEnchantment, Evocation, NecromancyImpose will, destroy resistance, and turn life or death into leverage.

The Contested School

Enchantment appears in both White and Black traditions by design. A White Robe asks whether magic can reinforce a choice without replacing it. A Black Robe asks how efficiently that choice can be replaced. The distinction is philosophical, but it is also mechanical: White Enchantments protect agency, courage, clarity, or agreement; Black Enchantments compel, suppress, or dominate.

Learning These Spells

These spells are intended primarily for Wizards of High Sorcery and characters taught directly by the Orders. Passing the Test opens the libraries of an Order; it does not place every spell in the wizard's spellbook. Individual spells are still learned, copied, awarded, stolen, discovered, or taught according to the normal rules of the campaign.

Entries identified as Tower Master secrets or Conclave secrets should normally be discoveries or plot rewards rather than routine level-up selections.

pages.name: Overreaching: The Price of the Test
pages.html:
A Wizard of High Sorcery can push a spell past the slot that holds it. The art permits this. It simply requires the caster to make up the difference out of themselves.

This is the mechanical inheritance of the Test. A candidate who has been made to pay a price once knows, in a way no book teaches, that magic will take what it is owed from whatever is nearest — and that the nearest thing is always the caster.

Only a wizard who has passed the Test may Overreach. Renegades cannot, apprentices cannot, and no amount of raw talent substitutes. This is the single largest mechanical reward for taking the Test in The Test of High Sorcery.

The Rule

When you cast a spell using a spell slot, you may declare that you are Overreaching. Choose 1, 2, or 3 additional levels. The spell takes effect as though cast using a slot of that higher level.

  • Declare before rolling anything. You cannot Overreach after seeing the result.
  • The effective level cannot exceed 9th.
  • You must be able to pay your Order's Price in full. If you cannot, you cannot Overreach.
  • The Price is paid immediately, whether or not the spell succeeds. It cannot be prevented, reduced, redirected, resisted, or negated by any means — including your own magic.
  • A spell cast this way still requires concentration as normal, and still uses the original slot.

There is no daily limit. The limit is what it costs you.

OrderThe PriceWhat it is
WhiteThe Silver TollYou take the harm yourself, and it does not heal.
RedLunitari's LedgerThe art is paid in its own currency, or in exhaustion.
BlackNuitari's DueVitality is spent — yours, or someone else's.

When It Is Worth It

Deliberately, almost never for damage. Overreaching a 5th-level slot to 8th adds about 10 points to a fireball and costs a White Robe 33. Anyone doing the arithmetic will stop doing it.

It is worth it where a level does something a die cannot:

  • reaching a spell level you do not have a slot for at all;
  • banishment, hold monster or polymorph at a level that catches a tougher creature;
  • an upcast healing or restoration when someone is about to die;
  • counterspell or dispel magic that must not fail;
  • a duration or target count that changes what is possible rather than how much it hurts.

The Price is flat per level and the benefit is not, so Overreaching is a tool for the one moment in a session that actually matters. That is the intent.

DM Note — Why This Exists

It gives every caster a lever they can pull at the worst moment, and every Order a different relationship with that lever. The White Robe bleeds. The Red Robe spends. The Black Robe decides whose it is.

That third one is the campaign in one mechanic. See Nuitari's Due.

pages.name: The Three Prices
pages.html:
The Silver Toll — White Robes

Solinari's servants are taught that a shield is only a shield if someone is standing behind it.

Price: you take 2d10 force damage per additional level, and your hit point maximum is reduced by the total rolled until you finish a long rest.

This damage cannot be prevented, resisted, or reduced. It is not an attack and does not trigger anything that responds to damage from a creature. If it reduces your hit point maximum to 0, you die, and Solinari does not intervene — you were told what this cost.

Silver Toll is the only Price that can be paid while unconscious, and it is the only one that can be paid by a caster with no spell slots left. A White Robe can always overreach. That is deliberate, and it is why they die doing it.

Lunitari's Ledger — Red Robes

The Red Robes hold that magic is neither given nor taken but exchanged, and that an unbalanced ledger is a debt that collects itself.

Price: immediately expend additional spell slots whose combined level equals twice the additional levels. Any shortfall costs you one level of exhaustion per level unpaid.

Additional levelsSlot levels owedExample payment
+12one 2nd, or two 1st
+24one 4th, or a 3rd and a 1st
+36one 6th, or a 4th and a 2nd

You choose how much to pay in slots and how much in exhaustion, and you may deliberately pay in exhaustion even with slots available. Doing so is regarded by the Order as either admirable or unstable depending on who is asked.

The Red Robe is the only caster who can overreach at no personal cost — provided they are rich enough in slots. A Red Robe late in a long day is as fragile as anyone.

Nuitari's Due — Black Robes

The black moon does not accept payment in effort or in currency. It accepts life.

Price: 3d10 necrotic damage per additional level. The damage cannot be prevented or reduced, and the victim's hit point maximum is reduced by the amount taken until they finish a long rest.

By default you pay it. But a Black Robe may instead take the Due from another creature within 30 feet that is one of the following:

  • willing;
  • grappled, restrained, paralyzed, unconscious, or incapacitated by you or an ally;
  • bound to you by an oath, contract, geas, or soul seal.

The creature does not get a saving throw. Nothing about this is difficult.

DM Note — This Is the Campaign

Nuitari's Due is the only Price with a choice in it, and the choice is whether the cost lands on you or on someone who cannot stop you.

Every use on an unwilling creature raises Raistlin Control by 1 — whether or not Raistlin knows, because the tracker measures what the party has demonstrated is acceptable, not what he has been told.

Using it on a willing creature raises nothing. Using it on yourself when a bound prisoner was standing right there lowers Control by 1, at most once per session.

Yes, this makes the Black Robe strictly the strongest overreacher, provided they have a prisoner. That is not an oversight. A Black Robe with a bound captive pays nothing at all, and the party will work that out within two sessions of acquiring one. What they do next is the information you actually want.

Do not comment on any of this at the table. Adjust the tracker silently and let the pattern become visible in how NPCs treat them.

pages.name: The Order Feats
pages.html:
Seven feats ship in the Wayreth — Orders & Feats compendium. Drag one onto a character sheet and it carries its own rules text.

The Three Order Feats

Wizard of High Sorcery (White Robe / Red Robe / Black Robe). This is what passing the Test grants. Each version gives the same four things, differing only in which moon and which Price:

  • Order spell access — the thirty spells of that Order, cantrips through 9th, as wizard spells.
  • Half time and half cost to scribe spells of your own Order into your book. Other Orders' spells cost the ordinary amount, and your Order will have opinions.
  • Moon sanction under Solinari, Lunitari or Nuitari.
  • Overreaching, paying the Silver Toll, Lunitari's Ledger or Nuitari's Due.
  • The robe itself: +1 spell save DC while worn.

These are granted, not chosen. Do not let a player take one at an ability score improvement. It is awarded on passing the Test and taken away if the Conclave revokes standing — which has happened twice in three hundred years and both times ended badly.

The Four Supporting Feats

FeatRequiresWhat it does
Conclave StandingAny Order featSecond Library access, one vault requisition per downtime, the Conclave's writ once per long rest, and renegade hunters who will parley first.
Marked by the TestAny Order feat+1 Int/Wis/Cha, your Mark's boon and cost both deepen, and one failed save per long rest can be turned into a success at 4d10 psychic and the Mark's cost again.
Moon-SwornAny Order featAlways know your moon's phase; one free upcast per long rest during high sanction; keep your top slot during low sanction; a free 5th-level spell on the night of alignment.
Renegade ArcanistRefused the Test+1 Int, scribe anything regardless of interdiction, resist divination that hunts you, recast a countered spell once per long rest. Cannot Overreach. No sanction either way.

Those three are ordinary feat choices and can be taken at an ability score improvement.

DM Note — Renegade Arcanist Is Not a Trap

A player who refuses the Test should not simply be worse off. Renegade Arcanist is deliberately strong in the areas the Orders restrict — unrestricted scribing is a genuine advantage over twenty levels, and the recast-on-counterspell is excellent.

What they lose is Overreaching, sanction, and the entire social apparatus. That is a real trade and the player should be able to see both halves of it before they decide.

pages.html:
Solinari's tradition is one of disciplined protection, truthful sight, and the defence of the mind's right to choose. White Robe magic is strongest when the wizard has something — or someone — to preserve.

See clearly. Stand between. Give strength without taking the choice away.

pages.name: Black Robe Spellbook
pages.html:
Nuitari's tradition treats magic as leverage: concentrated force, compelled obedience, stolen vitality, and the mastery of death as a resource rather than a boundary.

Power unused is merely possibility. The Black Robe concerns himself with what power can be made to do.

pages.name: Legacy Conversions
pages.html:
Thirty-one spells in this collection descend directly from the supplied 3.5e High Sorcery material. Their narrative identities remain intact, but the rules beneath them have been rebuilt for fifth edition.

The old spell is not preserved by copying every number. It is preserved when it creates the same decision, danger, or possibility at the table.

Conversion principle

Caster-Level Arithmetic

Ranges, durations, damage, and target counts based on caster level become fixed fifth-edition values or explicit spell-slot scaling.

Saving Throws

Will, Fortitude, and Reflex become Wisdom, Constitution, and Dexterity unless the fiction of the spell clearly attacks intellect or force of personality instead.

Spell Resistance

Spell Resistance is removed. Fifth edition's saving throws, attack rolls, concentration rules, legendary resistance, and bounded accuracy perform that balancing work.

Experience Costs and Permanent Penalties

XP expenditure becomes costly material components, once-per-rest restrictions, or explicit campaign limitations. Long-term ability drain and hard lockouts become repeat saves, long-rest recovery, remove curse, or greater restoration where appropriate.

Tower and Grove Secrets

The old Tower-grove protections remain intentionally specialised. Each has enough general utility to remain a legitimate spell while its original purpose remains the reason the Orders guard it.
